target.title: refactor(memory): drop redundant agent-id scoping from qmd collection names
target.body:
## Summary

- **What:** drop the redundant `-<agentId>` scoping from managed qmd collection names. Each agent has its **own isolated qmd index** (`agents/<agentId>/qmd/index.sqlite`), so collection names can't collide across agents — the agent-id suffix adds nothing but hardcodes the agent id into collection identifiers.
- **How:** remove `scopeCollectionBase` (and two now-dead path helpers, `isPathInsideRoot` / `canonicalizePathForContainment`); name default collections by their base (`memory-root`, `memory-dir`), the session collection `sessions`, and extra collections by their explicit name. Reverse the legacy migration to **scoped→unscoped** (`migrateLegacyScopedCollections` / `deriveLegacyScopedName`) so existing per-agent indexes migrate cleanly.
- **Why migration is cheap:** qmd collections are a **rebuildable derived index** (not user data), so the migration drops the stale scoped collection and lets the unscoped one be (re)created + reindexed — no import, no data loss (consistent with this repo's "prefer delete/drop/rebuild over import for cache").
- **Outcome:** stable, agent-agnostic collection names; net **−42 LOC** of production code for the de-scope itself (removes `scopeCollectionBase` + two now-dead path helpers in `backend-config.ts`).
- **Orphan cleanup:** the scoped→unscoped migration is **kind-gated**. Engine-owned collections (`memory`/`sessions`, whose base names are engine-generated and not user-suppliable) are removed even when their pattern has drifted from the current default; user-named (`custom`) collections keep the path+pattern guards and are **never** auto-deleted. Without this, a pattern-drifted legacy engine collection lingered as an orphan and was re-walked + re-embedded by every `qmd update` — a recurring reindex cost the migration otherwise shipped. (Trade-off, stated for transparency: for engine kinds this intentionally drops the prior "a user coincidentally named a collection like a legacy scoped name" guard — safe because those base names cannot be user-supplied; `custom` retains it.)
- **Disambiguated custom-name upgrade (ClawSweeper P1):** when two custom collections share a name, the shipped scoped names disambiguated as `<base>-<agentId>-<n>` (e.g. `notes-main`, `notes-main-2`), but the unscoped probe `deriveLegacyScopedName(<base>-<n>)` is `<base>-<n>-<agentId>` (`notes-2-main`) — so `migrateLegacyScopedCollections` missed the second orphan, and qmd then rejected the new unscoped collection on the same path+pattern, stranding it under the legacy name. `tryRebindConflictingCollection` now confirms the collection qmd names in the add-conflict via `qmd collection show` (the only command that surfaces the path, reusing `enrichLegacyCollectionPath`) and rebinds it when path **and** pattern match; a parsed name alone never removes a collection, so user-owned path guards are preserved.
- **Stacked on #91253 (per ClawSweeper):** the first commit is the path-aware qmd-rebind fix (#91253); the remaining commits are the de-scope, a docs + session-migration-test follow-up, and the kind-gated orphan cleanup. The rebind is **required** for the migration to be safe — without path-aware metadata, an upgraded index holding both a stale *unscoped* collection (old path) and a current *scoped* one could keep the stale unscoped target active; with the rebind folded in, the stale unscoped collection is rebound to the current path. Once #91253 lands, this rebases to drop that first commit.

## Linked context

Closes #91259

Depends on / folds in #91253 (path-aware qmd collection rebind) — the first commit of this PR.

Related: #91265 (an earlier PR toward the same proposal; this one folds in the path-aware rebind so existing scoped indexes migrate safely, adds an upgrade-case regression, and includes live before/after behavior proof).

Requested by a maintainer or owner? No — follows from the proposal in #91259.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: managed qmd collection names dropping the redundant `-<agentId>` suffix; existing per-agent indexes migrate scoped→unscoped; and orphaned engine-owned legacy collections are cleaned up.

Real environment tested: (A) a live, self-hosted OpenClaw gateway (macOS), backend `qmd` (`@tobilu/qmd` 2.5.2) running this build, against an agent whose index already held scoped collections; (B) a scratch per-agent index driven by the real `QmdMemoryManager` + the real `qmd` 2.5.2 binary for the orphan-cleanup case; (C) a scratch in-container→host rebind driven by the real `QmdMemoryManager` + real `qmd` 2.5.2 binary (the sandbox-mode transition).

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
```
# (A) live gateway — de-scope migration on an agent with existing scoped collections:
openclaw gateway restart
openclaw memory index --force --agent <agent>
sqlite3 <agent-qmd-index>.sqlite "select name,path from store_collections order by name;"

# (B) scratch index — seed two legacy scoped orphans (drifted pattern), run the engine (cli mode):
qmd collection add <ws>/memory --name memory-dir-<agent> --mask "**/*.txt"   # engine-owned (memory)
qmd collection add <ws>/notes  --name notes-<agent>      --mask "**/*.txt"   # user-owned   (custom)
# then QmdMemoryManager.create({ mode: "cli" }) runs the migration; list collections before/after.

# (C) sandbox-mode transition — seed a collection at a stale in-container root, run the engine:
qmd collection add <root>/home/node/.openclaw/teams/x/workspace --name workspace --mask "**/*.md"
# then QmdMemoryManager.create({ mode: "cli" }) with workspace=<host-root>; `qmd collection show workspace` before/after.
```

Evidence after fix:
```
# (A) live gateway (identifiers redacted):
# BEFORE (scoped names):
memory-root-<agent>   <WS>
memory-dir-<agent>    <WS>/memory
sessions-<agent>      <agent-state>/qmd/sessions
team-library-<agent>  <WS>/library/promoted
team-library          <WS-old>/library/promoted    # orphan duplicate
# AFTER (reindex):
memory-root / memory-dir / sessions / team-library  # all unscoped
# scoped (-<agent>) collections remaining: 0

# (B) scratch index, real qmd 2.5.2 + real engine (both orphans had a DRIFTED pattern):
# BEFORE:
memory-dir-proofagent  Pattern: **/*.txt   # engine-owned (memory)
notes-proofagent       Pattern: **/*.txt   # user-owned   (custom)
# AFTER (engine ran, mode=cli):
notes-proofagent       Pattern: **/*.txt   # LEFT  — user data never auto-deleted
memory-root / memory-dir / notes           # unscoped, engine-created from scratch
# memory-dir-proofagent : 1 -> 0  (engine-owned, removed)
# notes-proofagent      : 1 -> 1  (user-owned, preserved)

# (C) sandbox-mode transition, real qmd 2.5.2 + real engine:
# BEFORE: workspace -> .../home/node/.openclaw/teams/x/workspace   (stale in-container root)
# AFTER (engine ran, mode=cli): workspace -> .../host/workspace    (rebound to host root)
```

Observed result after fix: (A) all managed collections migrated to unscoped names (including `sessions`); `0` scoped collections remained; the prior orphan duplicate (`team-library` + `team-library-<agent>`) collapsed to a single `team-library`. (B) the engine-owned drifted-pattern orphan was removed while the user-owned one was preserved, and fresh unscoped collections (`memory-root`/`memory-dir`/`notes`) were created. (C) a collection pinned to a stale in-container path was rebound to the configured host workspace root.

What was not tested: launching an actual Docker sandbox container — the bind-mount + container-launch plumbing is OpenClaw platform infrastructure, outside this PR's diff. The in-container→host path transition this PR's code performs is proven with the real binary in (C) above and by a unit test (container→host rebind transition, #91253).

Proof limitations or environment constraints: (A) is redacted terminal output from a private fleet (paths/agent/team identifiers removed); (B) uses generic scratch identifiers and is reproducible by any maintainer on `qmd 2.5.2`.

Before evidence: shown inline in (A) above (the pre-reindex scoped names + orphan duplicate).

## Tests and validation

Commands run (clean checkout off `openclaw/openclaw` `main`, re-verified on the current head after the disambiguation fix):
- `pnpm test extensions/memory-core/src/memory` → **444 passed (40 files)**
- `pnpm test packages/memory-host-sdk` → **38 passed (9 files)**
- `pnpm check:test-types` (tsgo) → **clean, 0 errors**
- `oxfmt --check` + `oxlint` on the touched files → clean.

Regression coverage:
- Default + custom collection-name tests now assert the unscoped form.
- The unscoped→scoped migration tests were replaced with scoped→unscoped ones.
- **Upgrade-case regression (addresses the flagged compatibility risk):** an index holding BOTH a stale *unscoped* collection (old path) AND a current *scoped* one at the name switch → asserts the stale unscoped collection is rebound to the **current** path (via the folded-in `collection show` path enrichment), not left active.
- **Kind-gated orphan cleanup:** a rewritten migration-guard test — a `memory`-kind legacy scoped collection with a drifted pattern is now **removed** (genuinely fails against the pre-fix guard), while a `custom`-kind one with a drifted pattern is **left** — plus a contract test asserting every managed collection carries a `kind` (the safety gate depends on it).
- **Disambiguated custom-name upgrade regression:** two custom collections both named `notes` at different roots, with legacy `notes-<agentId>` / `notes-<agentId>-2` seeded in a real-`qmd`-shaped mock (name-only `collection list`, path-bearing `collection show`) → asserts the disambiguated orphan (`notes-<agentId>-2`) is removed and both unscoped collections (`notes`, `notes-2`) bind to their correct roots. Red against the pre-fix conflict path (the orphan is never removed), green after.

Multi-agent note: safe by construction — each agent has its own isolated qmd index, so unscoped names cannot collide across agents.

## Risk checklist

User-visible behavior change? Internal only — qmd collection identifiers (a derived index) change; no user-facing API/config change.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? Migration only: existing per-agent indexes migrate scoped→unscoped on the next `ensureCollections()` (drop stale scoped + recreate unscoped + reindex). No config keys changed.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? No.

Highest-risk area: the scoped→unscoped migration on existing indexes, and the kind-gated removal of legacy scoped collections.

How is that risk mitigated: removal only ever targets the exact derived legacy name `<base>-<agentId>` for a **desired** collection. For `custom` collections the path+pattern guards remain, so a user-named collection is never auto-deleted. For `memory`/`sessions` the base names are engine-generated and cannot be user-supplied, so the derived legacy name is unambiguously engine-owned; if such a collection is still configured it is simply re-added at the same path/pattern (net-zero, a reindex). qmd collections are rebuildable, so any dropped-then-recreated collection reindexes from source with no user-visible data loss.

## Current review state

Next action: maintainer review.

What is still waiting: CI + review.

Which bot or reviewer comments were addressed: ClawSweeper review findings on #91274 (docs example, session-migration coverage, scoped-duplicate upgrade case, orphan cleanup, and the disambiguated custom-name migration P1 — fixed via the show-verified conflict rebind).

target.title: fix(irc): chunk PRIVMSG on UTF-16 boundary to avoid lone surrogates
target.body:
**Summary:** Long IRC PRIVMSG payloads were chunked on raw UTF-16 indices, so an emoji straddling a chunk boundary was torn into lone surrogates — malformed UTF-8 on the wire and a garbled glyph for the recipient. This chunks on code-point boundaries so surrogate pairs are never split.

## What Problem This Solves

`connectIrcClient` in `extensions/irc/src/client.ts` splits long PRIVMSG payloads into chunks of at most `messageChunkMaxChars` (default 350). The split was a raw `chunk.slice(0, splitAt)` on the **UTF-16 string**. When the split index lands in the middle of an astral character — i.e. between the high and low halves of a surrogate pair (any emoji such as 🙂 `U+1F642`) — the chunk ends with a lone high surrogate and the next chunk begins with a lone low surrogate. That produces malformed UTF-8 on the wire and a broken/garbled emoji on the receiving client.

Trigger: a message of `"xxxxxxxxx🙂rest"` with `messageChunkMaxChars = 10`. The naive split at UTF-16 index 10 cuts the emoji in half (high `0xD83D` | low `0xDE42`).

## Fix

Add `sliceIrcPrivmsgChunk`, which slices on a safe UTF-16 boundary via the shared `sliceUtf16Safe` helper (`openclaw/plugin-sdk/text-utility-runtime`) so a surrogate pair is never split. Edge case: when a single leading code point already exceeds the chunk budget, `sliceUtf16Safe` would return empty; the helper detects a leading surrogate pair and emits it whole (`text.slice(0, 2)`) so chunking still advances instead of looping. `messageChunkMaxChars` is also clamped to a sane `Math.max(1, Math.floor(...))`.

## Evidence

Real IRC send/receive E2E proof, using a local TCP IRC server process and real TCP clients. This is not a `node:net` / `node:tls` mock.

The sender imported the PR branch's real `connectIrcClient` implementation and connected to `127.0.0.1`. A separate raw `net.Socket` IRC client joined the same channel and received the forwarded `PRIVMSG` chunks from the server. The proof forced `messageChunkMaxChars=10` with payload `"xxxxxxxxx🙂rest"`, placing the emoji at the chunk boundary.

```text

[server] READY host=127.0.0.1 port=37955

[server] recv NICK nick=oc_pr_receiver
[server] recv USER nick=oc_pr_receiver
[server] welcome nick=oc_pr_receiver
[server] recv JOIN nick=oc_pr_receiver channel=#oc-e2e
sender: real OpenClaw connectIrcClient nick=oc_pr_sender channel=#oc-e2e
[server] recv NICK nick=oc_pr_sender
[server] recv USER nick=oc_pr_sender
[server] welcome nick=oc_pr_sender
payload: "xxxxxxxxx🙂rest"

[server] recv JOIN nick=oc_pr_sender channel=#oc-e2e
[server] recv PRIVMSG from=oc_pr_sender target=#oc-e2e text="xxxxxxxxx" codeUnits=9 loneSurrogate=false
[server] fwd PRIVMSG from=oc_pr_sender to=oc_pr_receiver target=#oc-e2e

recv chunk 1: "xxxxxxxxx" codeUnits=9 containsEmoji=false loneSurrogate=false
recv chunk 2: "🙂rest" codeUnits=6 containsEmoji=true loneSurrogate=false

```

Result: each received `PRIVMSG` chunk is UTF-16 well-formed with no lone surrogate, the `🙂` emoji arrived intact in the second chunk, and the raw receiver's rejoined payload exactly matched the original message.

## Tests

`extensions/irc/src/client.surrogate.test.ts` drives the real `connectIrcClient` over a mocked socket and asserts (red before the fix, green after):

- `does not split an emoji surrogate pair across PRIVMSG chunks` — emoji at the budget boundary is not torn; no chunk contains a lone surrogate.
- `keeps a leading emoji whole when the UTF-16 budget is one code unit` — single-code-point-over-budget edge case emits the emoji whole and advances.
- `splits an all-emoji message into whole emoji when the budget is one code unit` — every chunk is well-formed.
- `still prefers a nearby space when splitting long PRIVMSG text` — confirms the existing word-boundary preference is preserved (no regression).

Each test runs the lone-surrogate regex `/[\uD800-\uDBFF](?![\uDC00-\uDFFF])|(?<![\uD800-\uDBFF])[\uDC00-\uDFFF]/` over every PRIVMSG body the client writes.

target.title: fix: user-pinned model falls back to global chain on quota exhaustion
target.body:
## Problem

When a user selects a model via \`/model <name>\`, \`modelOverride\` is stored in \`sessions.json\` with \`modelOverrideSource: \"user\"\`. The \`resolveEffectiveModelFallbacks\` function returns \`[]\` for user-sourced overrides, making \`hasFallbackCandidates = false\`.

When the pinned model hits a **long-term** failure (weekly/monthly quota exhaustion, subscription limit), every subsequent message fails with:

\`\`\`
⚠️ All models are temporarily rate-limited. Please try again in a few minutes.
\`\`\`

This is a complete outage — no recovery path short of manually editing \`sessions.json\`.

**Root cause** (\`src/agents/agent-scope.ts\`):

\`\`\`typescript
if (!canUseConfiguredFallbacks) {
  return [];  // disables entire fallback chain for user-pinned sessions
}
\`\`\`

**Reproduction:**
1. Use \`/model glm-5\` (or any model with a weekly quota)
2. Exhaust the weekly quota (error 1310 from zhipuai)
3. Every new message fails — even after gateway restart — because \`sessions.json\` persists \`modelOverride\` across sessions and new sessions inherit the pin

## Fix

Return the global fallback chain instead of \`[]\`. The user's intent when pinning a model is to **prefer** it, not to disable recovery when it's unavailable. The pinned model remains the **first** candidate and is always tried first.

For subagent sessions, the subagent-specific fallback chain is used (same as auto-selected subagents), rather than the generic agent/default chain.

## Behavior change

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| User-pinned model temporarily rate-limited | Error surfaced | Falls back to next model |
| User-pinned model quota exhausted (days/weeks) | Permanent outage | Falls back to next model |
| User-pinned subagent model quota exhausted | Permanent outage | Falls back to subagent fallback chain |
| No model pin / auto-fallback pin | Unchanged | Unchanged |

## Real behavior proof

Two occurrences captured in local gateway logs on 2026-05-30 (before this fix), both showing the same subagent \`zai/glm-5\` session hitting the weekly quota with zero fallback candidates:

**Occurrence 1 — 2026-05-30T13:14 CST**

Session \`b640381c\` (subagent \`a093b44d\`), run \`f6f7e336\`:

\`\`\`
# trajectory event: model.fallback_step
{
  "type": "model.fallback_step",
  "ts": "2026-05-30T05:14:09.631Z",
  "sessionKey": "agent:main:subagent:a093b44d-8405-4e1d-a3bd-00ccb1c2b7e5",
  "provider": "zai",
  "modelId": "glm-5",
  "data": {
    "fallbackStepFromModel": "zai/glm-5",
    "fallbackStepFromFailureReason": "rate_limit",
    "fallbackStepFromFailureDetail": "429 您已达到每周/每月使用上限，您的限额将在 2026-05-31 10:00:31 重置。",
    "fallbackStepChainPosition": 1,
    "fallbackStepFinalOutcome": "chain_exhausted"   // ← chain position 1 + exhausted = 0 candidates
  }
}
\`\`\`

Gateway log at the same moment:
\`\`\`
2026-05-30T13:14:09.778+08:00 [ws] ⇄ res ✗ agent errorCode=UNAVAILABLE
  errorMessage=FailoverError: ⚠️ API rate limit reached. Please try again later.
  runId=f6f7e336-85e2-4db7-825e-59ec76b32a07
\`\`\`

**Occurrence 2 — 2026-05-30T15:23 CST (2 hours later, same quota, still no fallback)**

Session \`f455173a\` (subagent \`90f819dc\`), run \`625ffb86\`:

\`\`\`
# trajectory event: model.fallback_step
{

target.title: fix(update): guard Windows task autostart during package updates
target.body:
## Summary
- disables enabled Windows Scheduled Task autostart while a managed package update replaces the OpenClaw package tree
- covers running, stopped, and unclassified installed task runtimes, including `--no-restart` stopped/unknown cases where the task can still logon-start during replacement
- re-enables only tasks this update actually disabled, before post-core handoff, restart handoff, blocked-update exits, or failed-update exits
- treats omitted `<Settings><Enabled>` in live Task Scheduler XML as enabled, matching native Windows output where enabled tasks are represented by absence of an explicit disabled state
- reports failed `/ENABLE` recovery if service stop fails after autostart was suspended, so the operator is not left with silently disabled logon autostart
- leaves startup-folder fallback installs, unavailable `schtasks`, missing tasks, unreadable XML state, and already-disabled tasks unchanged

Fixes #87993.

## Verification
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/daemon/schtasks.stop.test.ts src/cli/update-cli.test.ts -- --run` - 147 passed
- `node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/daemon/schtasks.ts src/daemon/schtasks.stop.test.ts src/cli/update-cli/update-command.ts src/cli/update-cli.test.ts`
- `node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/daemon/schtasks.ts src/daemon/schtasks.stop.test.ts src/cli/update-cli/update-command.ts src/cli/update-cli.test.ts`
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD && git diff --check`
- `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode branch --base origin/main` - clean, patch correct
- AWS Crabbox changed gate on rebased branch: `run_80f36e0c133e`, `pnpm check:changed` passed
- AWS Crabbox native Windows Task Scheduler XML proof: `run_16c0e77f1c9a`, `scheduled_task_disable_enable_xml_live=ok`
  - seeded a legacy-style LogonTrigger task with `PT3M` / `P9999D`
  - observed enabled live XML represented by absence of `<Settings><Enabled>false</Enabled>`
  - verified `/DISABLE` writes `<Settings><Enabled>false</Enabled>`
  - verified `/ENABLE` removes the explicit disabled state again
  - verified PT3M/P9999D repetition metadata survives disable/enable
- AWS Crabbox native Windows disabled-run probe: `run_373d5c3d81fc` observed `ERROR: The scheduled task "OCProof..." could not run because it is disabled.` The script intentionally failed because PowerShell promoted the expected stderr into a native-command error.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: Windows package updates no longer leave an enabled Scheduled Task free to relaunch the gateway while the package tree is being replaced. If the task was suspended and service stop then fails, failed `/ENABLE` recovery is now surfaced instead of hidden.

Real environment tested: Focused local regression tests on current branch SHA `da348c17f40`; AWS Crabbox Linux changed gate; AWS Crabbox native Windows Task Scheduler with a seeded legacy-style PT3M/P9999D task.

Exact steps or command run after this patch:
```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/daemon/schtasks.stop.test.ts src/cli/update-cli.test.ts -- --run
node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check src/daemon/schtasks.ts src/daemon/schtasks.stop.test.ts src/cli/update-cli/update-command.ts src/cli/update-cli.test.ts
node_modules/.bin/oxlint src/daemon/schtasks.ts src/daemon/schtasks.stop.test.ts src/cli/update-cli/update-command.ts src/cli/update-cli.test.ts
git diff --check origin/main...HEAD && git diff --check
.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode branch --base origin/main
node scripts/crabbox-wrapper.mjs run --provider aws --idle-timeout 90m --ttl 240m --timing-json --shell -- "pnpm check:changed"
```

Evidence after fix: Tests assert `/DISABLE` happens before service stop/package install and `/ENABLE` happens after install, before post-core fresh-process handoff. Tests also cover stopped and unknown installed task runtimes, `--no-restart` stopped/unknown runtimes, already-disabled task preservation, startup-fallback/no-schtasks no-op, Settings-level XML parsing, live-style omitted Settings Enabled defaults, NUL-separated XML output, and failed `/ENABLE` recovery after a service-stop failure. Native Windows proof showed Task Scheduler omits an explicit enabled setting for enabled tasks, writes explicit disabled state after `/DISABLE`, removes it after `/ENABLE`, and preserves legacy PT3M/P9999D repetition metadata.

Observed result after fix: package-update code suspends only a currently enabled Scheduled Task, resumes only if this update suspended it, and surfaces recovery failure if stop fails after suspension.

What was not tested: full native Windows OpenClaw package-update smoke remains unproven because the available AWS native Windows Crabbox image has `schtasks` but no Node/npm. WSL2 is not a touched runtime surface for this PR because WSL does not use the Windows Scheduled Task gateway service path.

target.title: fix: retry loopback probes without device identity after pairing repair
target.body:
## Summary

Fix a gateway probe edge case where a loopback probe with explicit gateway auth can get stuck in a pairing-repair path because the probe eagerly reuses cached device identity.

The new behavior is narrow:

- probe normally first, including cached device identity when available
- if a **loopback** probe with explicit auth fails before connect with a pairing-required repair response
- retry once without device identity, reusing the explicit token/password auth

This keeps the good path for paired device-aware probes, while avoiding repair-loop churn for local self-probes that already have usable explicit credentials.

## Why

I hit this on a dedicated worker Mac where the main `~/.openclaw` state was doing mixed duty:

- unattended worker/node state
- local CLI self-probe state

The dedicated profile gateways behaved fine, but the worker's plain main self-probe could repeatedly trigger device metadata repair requests instead of just using the explicit local gateway auth it already had.

That produced a noisy and misleading failure mode for `openclaw gateway probe` on loopback.

## Change details

- add a targeted retry path in `src/gateway/probe.ts`
- only trigger that retry when all of these are true:
  - loopback URL
  - explicit probe auth is present
  - a cached device identity was attached
  - the first attempt fails in `pairing_pending` with `PAIRING_REQUIRED`
  - failure happens before a successful connect/hello
- add a focused regression test in `src/gateway/probe.test.ts`

## Validation

Ran:

```bash
NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=8192 pnpm exec vitest run --config test/vitest/vitest.gateway.config.ts src/gateway/probe.test.ts
```

Result:

- `1 passed`
- `29 passed`

target.title: fix(infra): tolerate deleted cwd across startup, PATH, home-dir, and TUI [AI-assisted]
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Closes #73676. If a shell's working directory is removed before OpenClaw starts, Node's `process.cwd()` throws `ENOENT: uv_cwd`. CLI dotenv/PATH bootstrap and TUI startup used that call directly, so `openclaw tui` terminated before it could render a useful interface.

## Why This Change Was Made

Introduce one small nullable-CWD primitive, then keep the decision at each owner boundary:

- dotenv skips the vanished workspace file and continues global loading;
- PATH setup skips the opt-in project-local bin lookup rather than substituting HOME;
- required-home resolution uses valid configured sources or fails with actionable guidance;
- TUI workspace inference skips a missing cwd, autocomplete/auth use the package-root fallback, and local `!` commands refuse instead of silently running somewhere else.

This maintainer rewrite removes the redundant `is-main` refactor, the extra helper/test-routing surface, and the long fallback comments from the contributor patch. Normal cwd-present behavior is unchanged.

## User Impact

The CLI and full-screen TUI can start after their launch directory has been deleted. Security-sensitive project/PATH and local-shell semantics do not gain an implicit fallback. The unrecoverable no-home/no-cwd edge case now names the environment variables or directory action required.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox `tbx_01kwsmjrh13za4ghjn0kcrhfjt`, [run 28748684029](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/28748684029): 147 focused boundary/dotenv/TUI tests passed on the final rebased source.

- Same Testbox: built OpenClaw, started CLI and full-screen TUI in tmux directories removed before Node launch, observed version plus `gateway disconnected`, and observed no `uv_cwd`; command exited 0.

target.title: fix(voice-call): avoid OpenAI realtime double greeting
target.body:
Fixes #85846

## What Problem This Solves

OpenAI Realtime outbound calls could greet twice when caller audio arrived before `session.updated`: the provider drained that audio into server VAD before the explicit queued greeting had disabled automatic response creation.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Signal provider readiness before draining pre-ready caller audio, so the existing explicit greeting path establishes its response policy first.
- Suppress only server-VAD `create_response` while a manual response is active; retain interruption handling.
- Keep suppression through a queued retry and restore it only after the final response or terminal error.
- Correlate manual create/cancel failures with client event IDs so unrelated or stale Realtime errors cannot release suppression, and flush queued work after a correlated rejection.
- Share the turn-detection session-update builder across GA and Azure paths, without moving greeting content into session instructions.
- Remove redundant voice-call wrapper logic and tests now covered at the provider boundary.

No config, plugin API, or non-OpenAI realtime-provider behavior changes.

## User Impact

Outbound OpenAI Realtime calls produce one intended initial greeting even when the caller speaks immediately. Later caller interruptions still cancel the active response as before.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox: 58 OpenAI provider tests and 9 Talk runtime tests passed.
- Exact changed-surface gate passed: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/28752407321
- Live Twilio/OpenAI outbound call completed with one greeting.
- Direct authenticated OpenAI Realtime probe reached ready state, emitted three expected session updates, exactly one manual `response.create`, exactly one server response, zero errors, and returned audio plus transcript.
- Fresh autoreview found no actionable issues.
- Exact-head hosted CI passed at `53b9efa0a7118df9906c66999fc0580809c45baa`: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/28753065715

Known proof gaps: none for the changed surface.

target.title: feat(logbook): automatic work journal plugin with Control UI timeline tab
target.body:
Closes #99867

## What Problem This Solves

There is no way to look back at a day and see what you actually did on your machine. Time trackers log app names; they miss what the work was. Dayflow (MIT, standalone macOS app) proved the recipe — periodic screen capture, vision-model observation, timeline synthesis — but as a separate app its output is locked away from the assistant.

This PR adds **Logbook**, a bundled (disabled-by-default) plugin that turns screen snapshots from a paired node into a reviewable timeline of the day, surfaced in a new Control UI sidebar tab, with a daily-standup generator and timeline-grounded Q&A.

## Why This Change Was Made

OpenClaw already owns every capability the idea needs — node screen capture, media-understanding providers, plugin services, gateway RPC, plugin SQLite state, the dashboard. Composing them as a plugin keeps the data local, makes it queryable by the assistant later, and exercises existing seams:

- **Capture**: a plugin service invokes `screen.snapshot` (app nodes) or the new plugin-provided `logbook.snapshot` node-host command (headless macOS node hosts, backed by `screencapture`/`sips`) every `captureIntervalSeconds` (default 30s). A node-invoke policy adds `logbook.snapshot` to the default macOS allowlist while the plugin is enabled. Identical consecutive frames are marked idle and excluded from analysis.
- **Two-stage analysis** (Dayflow-style): elapsed windows (default 15 min, split at >2 min gaps) go to a structured-extraction vision model (`api.runtime.mediaUnderstanding.extractStructuredWithModel`, e.g. `codex/gpt-5.5`) producing timestamped observations; observations plus a 45-minute lookback of existing cards are revised into 10-60 min timeline cards via `api.runtime.llm.complete` (default agent model), with one JSON-repair retry. Cards are a revisable draft: later batches may restructure the recent window.
- **Storage**: plugin-owned SQLite (`node:sqlite`, same pattern as memory-core/imessage) under `<state-dir>/logbook/`; frames pruned after `retentionDays` (default 14); batches stuck in `running` reset to `pending` on restart.
- **UI**: new `Logbook` tab following the Workboard/Dreams precedent (core view calling plugin-registered `logbook.*` gateway methods; plugin-disabled callout when off). Timeline cards with category colors, keyframe snapshots, distraction chips; day stats; standup generator; ask-your-day box.

Architecture notes: owner boundary respected (all product logic in `extensions/logbook`; the core diff is generic tab wiring + i18n). No new core config; plugin config has 8 clamped keys. Raw SQL is plugin-local DDL plus prepared statements, matching existing extension storage (the shared Kysely helpers are core-only).

## User Impact

- Off by default; no behavior change until `openclaw plugins enable logbook`.
- Once enabled: the Logbook tab shows the day as expandable activity cards with focus/category stats, one-click standup notes, and natural-language recall over the tracked day.
- Privacy: frames and the timeline stay on the gateway host; images leave only as analysis input to the operator-chosen model; the headless capture command is only advertised/allowlisted while the plugin is enabled.

## Evidence

- Unit tests: `extensions/logbook/src/analyze.test.ts` (time parsing, JSON repair contract, overlap trimming, batch windowing/gap split, sampling, keyframe pick) and `extensions/logbook/src/store.test.ts` (idle exclusion, crash recovery, revision-window replacement, stats, retention pruning) — 21 tests green via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/logbook`.
- Contract suites green: `src/plugins/contracts/package-manifest.contract.test.ts`, `src/plugins/contracts/extension-runtime-dependencies.contract.test.ts`, `src/plugins/bundled-plugin-naming.test.ts`, `test/extension-import-boundaries.test.ts`.
- `pnpm build` green (bundled plugin dist + control UI assets); `pnpm tsgo` + `pnpm tsgo:extensions` green; scoped oxlint green; `pnpm ui:i18n:sync` regenerated locales.
- **Live end-to-end on macOS** (isolated-state dev gateway + headless node host from this branch): node paired with `logbook.snapshot` in its approved surface; real screen frames captured every 10s (19+ frames, idle detection active); analysis batches ran against real `codex/gpt-5.5` (`chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex/responses` transport) producing timestamped observations and merged timeline cards that correctly described the on-screen work; the Logbook tab rendered cards with keyframe snapshots, day stats (focus bar, categories, apps), a generated Daily Standup (Done/Today/Blockers), and an answered ask-your-day question. Live-test screenshots contain personal screen content and were reviewed locally instead of being attached.
- The live test also hardened the plugin: node-invoke policy allowlisting, `node.invoke` payload-envelope unwrapping, node-inventory diagnostics in capture errors, and config-snapshot loading for the tab were all found and fixed against the running gateway.

Release-note context: feat(plugins): add Logbook automatic work journal plugin with Control UI timeline tab (screen snapshots via paired nodes, Dayflow-style two-stage analysis, daily standup, ask-your-day).

target.title: fix(feishu): route chat tools through contextual accounts
target.body:
﻿Related: #96657

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where multi-account Feishu users could run `feishu_chat` from the wrong configured account.

`feishu_chat` covers the `info`, `members`, and `member_info` actions. Those actions are account-sensitive because chat IDs, member IDs, and visible membership data belong to the Feishu app/tenant that can access them. Before this PR, chat registration checked only the first enabled account and every chat client was created from that same account, so execution context such as `agentAccountId: "b"` could still call Feishu through account `a`.

This caused two concrete failures:

- a contextual chat call for account `b` could use account `a` when both accounts enabled chat;
- `feishu_chat` could fail to register when the first account disabled chat even though a later enabled account allowed it.

This PR is intentionally narrower than #96657. It only aligns `feishu_chat` with the existing Feishu tool-account resolver and does not claim to fix every non-inbound Feishu routing path.

## Why This Change Was Made

`feishu_chat` now follows the same resolver pattern as neighboring Feishu tools: registration checks whether any enabled account exposes chat, and execution creates the client through `createFeishuToolClient` with the current tool context.

The Feishu API calls, request payloads, response shape, configured secrets, and required Feishu/Lark scopes are unchanged. The account precedence is explicit: `accountId` parameter, then contextual `agentAccountId`, then the existing resolver fallback.

## User Impact

Single-account Feishu setups keep the same behavior.

Multi-account setups now route chat/member lookups through the selected contextual account instead of silently using the first enabled account. If the selected contextual account has `tools.chat` disabled, the tool fails closed with the existing disabled-tool error instead of falling back across accounts or tenants.

## Evidence

Focused regression coverage verifies:

- contextual `agentAccountId` selects the matching chat account;
- explicit `accountId` overrides the contextual account;
- disabled contextual chat accounts fail closed;
- chat registers when only a later configured account enables chat.

Redacted live/staged proof was gathered on 2026-06-30 with two local Feishu/Lark profiles managed by `lark-cli`. Secrets, access tokens, open IDs, chat IDs, tenant keys, group names, and member names were not included in the PR.

```text
live provider check:
- profile a: bot identity ready, chat get returned expected chat fields
- profile b: bot/user identities ready, chat list/get returned expected chat fields

staged OpenClaw production-router check:
- registeredFeishuChat: true
- contextAgentAccountId "b" -> selectedAccount "b"
- contextAgentAccountId "a" with account a chat disabled -> failedClosed true
- errorClass: Feishu Chat tools are disabled for account "a"
```

Validation:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/feishu/src/chat.test.ts extensions/feishu/src/tool-account-routing.test.ts` - passed, 2 files / 32 tests
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json --incremental --tsBuildInfoFile .artifacts/tsgo-cache/extensions-test-local-feishu-chat-slim.tsbuildinfo` - passed
- `pnpm test:extension feishu` - passed, 73 files / 979 tests

target.title: fix(heartbeat): skip plugin bootstrap and bundled fallback during delivery target resolution
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes a heartbeat wake-loop latency regression where delivery-target resolution blocks for ~60s per tick when the configured channel plugin is not already in the active runtime registry.

### Background

Commit [`6470bb7625`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/6470bb7625) (fix(heartbeat): bootstrap plugin session targets, #93630) solved a real problem: when a user configured `heartbeat.target` to a channel id that was not in the built-in known-deliverable-channel list (e.g. a third-party plugin id), `normalizeDeliverableOutboundChannel()` returned `undefined` and the target was silently dropped to `"none"`.

The fix called `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin({ allowBootstrap: true })` in the heartbeat delivery-target path. However, this triggers `resolveRuntimePluginRegistry()` → `loadOpenClawPlugins()`, which scans **all** installed plugins — not just the target channel.

### Root cause analysis

The `bootstrapOutboundChannelPlugin` guard in `channel-bootstrap.runtime.ts` has a `bootstrapAttempts` Set that caches per `(registryVersion, channel)` key:
- **Successful bootstrap**: key stays cached → subsequent ticks skip instantly
- **Failed bootstrap** (plugin not installed / config issue / transient failure): key is deleted → every tick re-runs the full plugin scan

This is the pathological case: a misconfigured or not-yet-installed heartbeat plugin channel causes repeated ~60s scans on every wake tick. The probe measurement confirmed:

```
Before (allowBootstrap: true,  no plugin): 73,308ms
After  (allowBootstrap: false, no plugin):   5.2ms
Pre-activation bootstrap (cold scan):           739ms (once at startup)
```

### When this bug is triggered

1. `heartbeat.target` is not `"none"` or `"last"`
2. The target channel is not in the active runtime registry
3. `heartbeat.to` is set (non-empty)

## Why This Change Was Made

Two-part fix:

### Part 1: Hot path optimization (original PR)

Three heartbeat-path call sites in `targets.ts` now pass `allowBootstrap: false, allowBundledFallback: false`. A new `allowBundledFallback` parameter is added to `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin` (default `true`) so hot paths can skip both the bootstrap scan AND the `getBundledChannelPlugin` lazy-load fallback.

### Part 2: Startup pre-activation (new — addresses review feedback)

A new `preactivateHeartbeatChannelPlugins()` function in `src/infra/outbound/heartbeat-pre-activate.ts` runs **once at gateway startup** (in `activateGatewayScheduledServices`, before `startHeartbeatRunner`). It reads the heartbeat config and, for non-standard plugin channel targets, calls `resolveOutboundChannelPlugin({ allowBootstrap: true })` to load the plugin into the active registry before the wake loop starts.

This preserves the delivery compatibility that PR #93630 established — external plugin channel heartbeat targets still get bootstrapped — but moves the bootstrap cost from the hot path (every tick) to startup (once).

Standard deliverable channels (telegram, discord, etc.) and targets of `"none"`/`"last"` are no-ops in pre-activation.

## User Impact

- **Normal deployment (plugin active)**: No change — plugin found in registry, <10ms resolution both before and after
- **Plugin not yet active** (external channel, delayed activation): Pre-activation resolves it at startup (~135–739ms once) instead of every heartbeat tick (~60s each). Delivery works.
- **Plugin not installed / misconfigured**: Fast fail at startup (best-effort bootstrap) and fast fail on hot path — no repeated scans

## Compatibility

- `allowBundledFallback` defaults to `true` — all non-heartbeat callers unchanged
- Pre-activation is a no-op for standard channel targets and `target: none/last`
- `resolveOutboundTarget` (general-purpose outbound) continues to pass `params.allowBootstrap` through transparently

## Evidence

### Unit tests (92/92 passed)
```
src/infra/outbound/targets.test.ts                  85 passed
src/infra/outbound/heartbeat-pre-activate.test.ts    7 passed
```

### Probe timing (isolated vitest)
```
Pre-activation bootstrap (cold scan):  739ms (external-channel)
Pre-activation bootstrap (cold scan):  135ms (plugin-channel)
Hot path (allowBootstrap: false):       <10ms (registry lookup)
```

### Lint / type checks
```
oxlint:  clean
tsgo:    clean (check:test-types)
format:  clean (oxfmt --check)
build:   clean (pnpm build)
```

### Review response

ClawSweeper review ([#100377](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/100377#issuecomment-4886719486)) identified that removing bootstrap from the hot path could drop delivery for external plugin channels not yet in the active registry. Startup pre-activation addresses this by resolving those plugins once before the wake loop starts, preserving the delivery compatibility of #93630 while keeping the hot path free of plugin scans.

target.title: fix(security): suppress unhandled stdout/stderr stream errors in install policy
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`runPolicyCommand` attaches `data` listeners to `child.stdout` and `child.stderr`, but does not attach `error` listeners. If either stream emits an `error` event, the unhandled error can crash the process or leave the policy command hanging.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add no-op `error` handlers to both stdout and stderr streams before the data handlers, mirroring the existing stdin error handling pattern. This prevents unhandled stream errors from propagating as uncaught exceptions.

## User Impact

More robust install policy execution: transient stream read errors no longer crash the OpenClaw process during skill/plugin installs.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test in `src/security/install-policy.test.ts` that mocks `spawn`, emits `error` events on both stdout and stderr, and verifies `runInstallPolicy` still resolves successfully.
- Verified the test fails on `main` with an unhandled `Error: stdout read failed` and times out, and passes with this fix.
- `oxlint` passes on the changed files.

## Why This Change Was Made

Cron finalization now treats a delivery-requested embedded run with no final payload or synthesized text as a cron run error instead of passing it into the silent delivery path. The guard preserves intentional silent replies, message-tool/source deliveries that already satisfied the target, and committed terminal progress such as deterministic approval prompts, accepted child sessions, or successful cron adds, so this does not change explicit no-reply, already-delivered, approval-pending, or handoff-only flows.

## User Impact

Operators and channel users now get an observable cron failure state for empty final assistant completions instead of a dark lane where the job is marked complete but no reply reaches the destination.

## Evidence

- Added focused regressions for a completed embedded run with delivery requested and no final payload. They assert the plain empty completion and unverified/off-target message-tool attempts become `error` with no dispatch, while deterministic approval prompts, accepted child-session handoffs, and successful cron-add completions are not misclassified as cron errors.
- Focused regression passed: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.cron.config.ts src/cron/isolated-agent/run.meta-error-status.test.ts` (10 tests).
- Near-real cron proof passed using qa-lab with qa-channel, a real gateway child process, and the mock-openai provider. The proof forced a delivery-requested isolated cron run whose mock model exhausted into an empty visible response; the run log showed `status=error`, `delivery=not-delivered`, and the qa-channel received one failure notification instead of the normal `EMPTY-EXHAUSTED-OK` success reply.
- Live cron proof passed using qa-lab with qa-channel, a real gateway child process, and live-frontier `claude-cli/opus`. The run stored a one-minute cron reminder, forced execution, completed via the cron path, and observed the QA channel delivery marker `QA-CRON-5df256c5`.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:core:test` passed.

target.title: [codex] fix discord missing voice state handling
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Discord returns REST error code 10065 when a guild member has no current voice state. OpenClaw treated that normal disconnected state as a command/gateway failure. The original patch also treated every HTTP 404 as absent, which could hide unrelated unknown-guild, unknown-channel, permission, or transport failures.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Discord plugin now recognizes only the provider's semantic `Unknown Voice State` code, with a narrow explicit-message fallback for legacy error shapes. Guild status and voice manager lookup share that predicate; generic 404 handling is removed.

## User Impact

Voice status for a disconnected Discord user returns an explicit absent/disconnected result. Other Discord REST errors continue to surface for diagnosis. No configuration or command changes are required.

## Evidence

- Live authenticated Discord REST proof returned code 10065 for a disconnected member and preserved code 10004 for an invalid guild.
- Official Discord API error documentation and `discord-api-types` distinguish those error codes.
- Focused Blacksmith Testbox run passed 127 manager and send tests: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/28749940176
- Tests cover active state, code 10065, the legacy explicit message, code 10004, status-only HTTP 404, and generic failures.
- Fresh Codex autoreview found no actionable issues before exact-head sync; exact-head gates are rerunning on the rebased branch.

## Implementation

- Add one internal Discord REST predicate for unknown voice state.
- Reuse it in guild status and voice manager paths.
- Preserve every non-10065 exception.
- Add a changelog entry thanking @asock.

target.title: fix(codex): isolated cron reports Codex startup stalls
target.body:
## Summary

What problem does this PR solve?

The root cause fixed here is a Codex app-server startup lifecycle timeout boundary: OpenClaw started the outer startup watchdog before Codex `initialize`, but the shared/isolated Codex client startup path did not receive the remaining startup deadline for that first required protocol request. When `client.initialize()` stalled after earlier startup work had consumed time, the broader startup watchdog could win first and surface a generic startup / isolated cron setup timeout instead of the blocked Codex initialize phase.

Why does this matter now?

For isolated cron runs routed through Codex, a stall before `thread/start` can currently look like `isolated agent setup timed out before runner start`, which hides the protocol phase that actually owns the failure once startup has reached `initialize`. The reporter's #84567 evidence proves the user-visible isolated cron setup timeout, `openai/gpt-5.5` / Codex routing, and a live idle Codex worker; it does not by itself prove the reporter-account run was already inside `client.initialize()`. The older #64744 evidence plus the deterministic proofs here cover the specific initialize lifecycle boundary.

What is the intended outcome?

Root-cause lifecycle fix for the Codex initialize timeout boundary: carry the startup deadline into the Codex app-server client factory, consume it only around `client.initialize()`, let the initialize timeout win before the outer watchdog, and stop connection-closed retries after the startup watchdog has already abandoned the attempt.

What is intentionally out of scope?

This does not change live OAuth auth selection, model routing, successful Codex app-server startup behavior, post-`thread/start` turn execution, user config, schema, protocol payloads, or public APIs. It also does not claim a full reporter-account live OpenAI OAuth recurring cron/provider turn.

What does success look like?

For runs that have reached Codex `initialize`, a stalled initialize request fails as `codex app-server initialize timed out` before `thread/start`, while pre-initialize factory/start-context hangs still report the generic startup timeout and successful initialize paths keep their existing behavior.

What should reviewers focus on?

Review the root invariant and risk boundary: `initialize` is the first required Codex protocol request before `thread/start`, so the remaining startup deadline must be enforced at that lifecycle owner instead of being left to a later generic startup watchdog. The timeout/retry change is intentionally narrow: only `client.initialize()` consumes the derived deadline, and connection-closed retries stop only after startup has already been abandoned.

- **Fix classification:** Root-cause Codex startup lifecycle and diagnostic-boundary fix for the `initialize` phase.
- **Maintainer-ready confidence:** High for the pre-`thread/start` initialize stall boundary and the issue-shaped isolated cron runner route. Remaining external proof is a full reporter-account live OpenAI OAuth recurring cron/provider turn; this body states that boundary instead of claiming it.
- **Root cause:** OpenClaw's Codex startup owner created a single outer startup deadline, but the shared/isolated client startup owner did not receive that remaining deadline for the first Codex protocol request, `client.initialize()`. That mismatch let the generic startup watchdog own failures that had already reached the initialize lifecycle boundary.
- **Why this is root-cause fix:** The patch moves timeout ownership to the source lifecycle owner by passing an initialize deadline through the internal client factory options and consuming it only at `client.initialize()`. That fixes the root invariant that the first protocol request must complete or fail inside the existing startup budget, rather than masking the symptom after a generic cron setup timeout has already been reported.
- **Patch quality notes:** Timeout/retry changes are bounded: the initialize deadline is only consumed by the shared/isolated `client.initialize()` phase, callers that omit it keep the old factory-wide timeout behavior, pre-initialize factory hangs stay on the generic startup-timeout path, and retries stop only after the outer startup watchdog has abandoned startup.
- **What did NOT change:** OAuth profile selection, provider/model routing, successful Codex app-server startup, post-`thread/start` runtime behavior, public config, schema, protocol payloads, and public APIs.
- **Architecture / source-of-truth check:** The source-of-truth boundary is the Codex app-server lifecycle contract: `initialize` must complete before `thread/start`. OpenClaw now enforces the existing startup budget at that protocol lifecycle boundary instead of post-processing downstream cron setup errors.
- **Target test file:** `extensions/codex/src/app-server/attempt-startup.test.ts` and `src/cron/isolated-agent.codex-app-server.test.ts`.
- **Scenario locked in:** The regression suite locks the stalled real-stdio initialize boundary, the pre-initialize generic startup-timeout boundary, abandoned-startup cleanup, connection-closed retry ownership after abandonment, and the real isolated cron `agentTurn` route for `openai/gpt-5.5` with the `openai-codex:default` profile id.
- **Why this is the smallest reliable guardrail:** The production change is limited to internal startup deadline wiring and retry ownership; the new cron proof uses the real isolated cron runner plus a Codex app-server protocol harness to exercise the issue-shaped route deterministically without requiring reporter-only OAuth credentials.

## Linked context

Which issue does this close?

This PR is related to #84567 and #64744. It does not use an auto-closing keyword because #84567 still has a reporter-account live OAuth cron/provider proof gap.

Which issues, PRs, or discussions are related?

Related #84567 and #64744. #84567 is the isolated cron setup-timeout report; #64744 provides older Codex initialize-hang context.

Was this requested by a maintainer or owner?

No direct maintainer request; this is a focused root-cause repair for linked bug reports and ClawSweeper review signals.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Stalled real stdio Codex initialize is bounded before `thread/start` and reports the initialize phase error.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux, Node `v22.22.0`, OpenClaw worktree after this patch, with a real stdio child process spawned through the Codex app-server client startup path.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```bash
pnpm exec tsx <evidence>/real-stdio-stalled-initialize-proof.ts
```

- **Evidence after fix (screenshot, recording, terminal capture, console output, redacted runtime log, linked artifact, or copied live output):** copied output from the real-stdio proof:

- **What was not tested:** This proof does not execute a live model turn, a real recurring cron fire against the reporter's account, or a live reporter OAuth refresh.
- **Proof limitations or environment constraints:** The remaining proof question is maintainer acceptance of lifecycle/root-cause boundary evidence versus requiring a full reporter-account live OpenAI OAuth recurring cron/provider turn.

## Tests and validation

Which commands did you run?

- `pnpm exec vitest run extensions/codex/src/app-server/attempt-startup.test.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/shared-client.test.ts`

What regression coverage was added or updated?

target.title: Add per-agent sandbox session visibility override feature
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: sandboxed session tools always applied the default sandbox session visibility clamp before considering the requesting agent, so `agents.list[].sandbox.sessionToolsVisibility` could be configured but was not consistently honored.
- Runtime impact: operators could not safely give one named sandboxed agent full configured session visibility while keeping other sandboxed agents clamped to spawned sessions.
- Change: session visibility resolution now derives the requester agent first, checks that agent's sandbox override, and falls back to `agents.defaults.sandbox.sessionToolsVisibility` only when no per-agent override exists.
- Compatibility: existing configs keep the same default `"spawned"` clamp unless a named agent explicitly sets `sandbox.sessionToolsVisibility`.

## User-Visible Behavior

New optional per-agent config:

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaults": {
      "sandbox": { "sessionToolsVisibility": "spawned" }
    },
    "list": [
      { "id": "tony", "sandbox": { "sessionToolsVisibility": "all" } }
    ]
  }
}
```

For sandboxed session tools, precedence is:

```text
agents.list[].sandbox.sessionToolsVisibility
agents.defaults.sandbox.sessionToolsVisibility
default spawned clamp
```

## Security Impact

- Data access scope can broaden only for an explicitly named sandboxed agent.
- The global/default sandbox behavior remains clamped to spawned sessions.
- Existing `tools.sessions.visibility` and `tools.agentToAgent` policy checks still apply; this does not bypass cross-agent policy.
- No secrets, credentials, network calls, shell execution, or gateway auth behavior changed.

## Files in This PR

- `CHANGELOG.md` - records the user-facing runtime/config behavior change.
- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md` - documents per-agent sandbox session visibility.
- `docs/gateway/config-tools.md` - documents session tool visibility and sandbox override precedence.
- `docs/tools/multi-agent-sandbox-tools.md` - documents multi-agent sandbox session tool behavior.
- `src/agents/openclaw-tools.ts` - wires requester identity into session tool construction.
- `src/agents/tools/session-status-tool.ts` - applies requester-aware sandbox visibility to `session_status`.
- `src/agents/tools/sessions-access.ts` - centralizes requester-aware sandbox visibility resolution.
- `src/agents/tools/sessions-helpers.ts` - forwards requester context through shared session helper wiring.
- `src/agents/tools/sessions-history-tool.ts` - applies requester-aware visibility to `sessions_history`.
- `src/agents/tools/sessions-list-tool.ts` - applies requester-aware visibility to `sessions_list`.
- `src/agents/tools/sessions-send-tool.ts` - applies requester-aware visibility to `sessions_send`.
- `src/agents/openclaw-tools.session-status.test.ts` - covers requester-aware `session_status` behavior.
- `src/agents/openclaw-tools.sessions-visibility.test.ts` - covers tool-factory wiring for the override.
- `src/agents/openclaw-tools.sessions.test.ts` - covers end-to-end session tool behavior through the OpenClaw tool factory.
- `src/agents/tools/sessions-access.test.ts` - covers access-layer override/fallback resolution.

target.title: feat: expose rawBody on user messages in plugin hook events
target.body:
### Summary

Add `rawBody` field to user messages in `agent_end`, `before_prompt_build`, and `before_agent_start` (legacy) hook events. This provides plugins with the original user input before channel structural context, `buildInboundUserContextPrefix()` metadata, and prompt-build hook injections are prepended.

### Motivation

Plugin hooks receive `event.messages` where user message `content` includes OpenClaw-injected metadata (timestamps, channel info, sender IDs) and other hook injections (e.g., memory context). Plugins that process user content for purposes like memory extraction, summarization, or analytics must parse and strip this metadata — a fragile approach since the format varies by channel, chat type, and OpenClaw version.

PR #51502 already established the precedent of using `RawBody` instead of `Body` to avoid passing envelope metadata to LLM processing. This PR extends that principle to plugin hook events.

### Changes

- Compute `rawBodyForHooks` from `CommandBody ?? RawBody ?? Body` in the channel message handler — the clean user text without @mentions, sender labels, or message annotations
- Thread `rawBody` through the run params chain: `get-reply-run.ts` → `runReplyAgent` → `runAgentTurnWithFallback` → `runEmbeddedPiAgent` → `runEmbeddedAttempt`
- Include `rawBody` in hook event objects for `before_prompt_build`, `before_agent_start`, and `agent_end`
- Add `rawBody` to `FollowupRun` type so the value survives queueing/deferred runs
- `rawBody` is `undefined` for non-channel runs (CLI, heartbeat, cron)
- **Steer race fix** (`86ebda8b`): Thread `rawBody` through the steer queue path so steered injections on non-Telegram channels refresh the active embedded run's hook context

### Backward Compatibility

- Additive optional field only — no breaking changes
- Plugins can feature-detect `rawBody` and fall back to `content`:
  ```typescript
  const userText = event.rawBody ?? extractText(lastUser.content);
  ```
- Plugin SDK API baseline unchanged (no drift)

### Use Case

Memory plugins send user+assistant pairs to backend for memory extraction. Without `rawBody`, the plugin must regex-strip injected XML blocks and cannot remove inbound metadata, causing noisy "memories" from message IDs and timestamps. With `rawBody`, the plugin gets clean user input directly.

### Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: Plugin hook events (`before_prompt_build`, `agent_end`) now expose `event.rawBody` containing clean user-input text (22 chars) instead of requiring plugins to parse the metadata-decorated `messages[-1].content` (411 chars). Non-channel origins (heartbeat, cron, exec-event) correctly emit `rawBody: undefined`. Steered injections on non-Telegram channels now refresh `rawBody` via the steer queue path.

Real environment tested: Linux 6.17.0-1013-aws (arm64), Node v22.22.2, OpenClaw 2026.5.20, Bedrock `global.anthropic.claude-opus-4-7` (us-east-1, IAM role auth), Telegram bot `@oc_jmu_bot` via long-poll, custom probe plugin (`rawbody-probe`) using `definePluginEntry` + `api.on("before_prompt_build")` + `api.on("agent_end")`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Built from PR HEAD (`git rev-parse HEAD` = `29e89cfb84`), ran `pnpm build`, started gateway with `node openclaw.mjs gateway --allow-unconfigured --port 18799 --bind loopback --auth none --verbose`. Sent Telegram DM "hello rawbody test 004" to `@oc_jmu_bot`. Triggered heartbeat via `node openclaw.mjs system event --text "..." --mode now --url ws://127.0.0.1:18799 --token anonymous --json`. Ran unit tests: `pnpm exec vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/get-reply-run.media-only.test.ts -t "rawBody hook gating" --reporter=verbose`.

Evidence after fix:
```
Case A — Channel happy path (Telegram DM):
[rawbody-probe] runId    = 4c1c5a9b-8e2c-405f-b6f3-d2246e4912cc
[rawbody-probe] trigger  = user
[rawbody-probe] rawBody  = "hello rawbody test 004"   (22 chars)
[rawbody-probe] lastUser = "Conversation info (untrusted metadata):\n...
                            hello rawbody test 003"   (411 chars)
[rawbody-probe] equal    = false
[rawbody-probe] eventKeys = prompt,messages,rawBody

Case B — Heartbeat origin:
[rawbody-probe] runId    = 40d31407-6882-4f23-bdc7-85ba18fb5a41
[rawbody-probe] trigger  = heartbeat
[rawbody-probe] rawBody  = <undefined>
[rawbody-probe] lastUser = "[OpenClaw heartbeat poll]"
[rawbody-probe] eventKeys = messages,success,error,durationMs,rawBody,runId

Unit tests after fix (6/6 pass):
✓ passes user text as rawBody for telegram channel runs       (62ms)
✓ gates rawBody to undefined for heartbeat runs               (2ms)
✓ gates rawBody to undefined for cron-event runs              (1ms)
✓ gates rawBody to undefined for exec-event runs              (1ms)
✓ prefers CommandBody over Body for channel rawBody           (1ms)
✓ threads rawBody through steer path for non-telegram channels (3ms)
Test Files  1 passed
     Tests  6 passed
```

Observed result after fix: `event.rawBody` on `before_prompt_build` and `agent_end` contains the exact 22-char clean user input for channel runs. Non-channel origins correctly emit `undefined`. The steer path unit test confirms `followupRun.rawBody` is threaded through for non-Telegram channels (discord provider).

What was not tested: Live steer-race reproduction on Discord/Slack/WhatsApp channels (Telegram's `serializeImmediate: true` prevents triggering the steer path live). The steer fix is covered by the new unit test which mocks `isEmbeddedPiRunStreaming = true` and asserts `rawBody` propagation. No multi-user concurrency test was performed.

target.title: fix(cron): stop fallback attempts when cron budget is exhausted
target.body:
## Problem

When a cron job's primary model times out near the cron deadline, the fallback model is started but immediately killed by the same cron timeout — receiving effectively 0ms to make an LLM request. The fallback never gets a fair chance to respond, and the user sees a misleading `cron: job execution timed out` error attributed to the fallback model.

**Observed in production logs (2026-03-22):**

```
[08:10:30.733] anthropic/claude-opus-4-6 attempt=1/2 reason=unknown err='Request was aborted.' duration=28667ms
[08:10:30.735] openai-codex/gpt-5.4    attempt=2/2 reason=timeout err='cron: job execution timed out' duration=0ms
```

The cron timeout wraps the entire fallback chain. When the primary model consumes most of the budget, the fallback model is allocated ~0ms and fails immediately.

## Solution

1. **Propagate the cron deadline** (`deadlineAtMs`) from `executeJobCoreWithTimeout` through the cron service state down to `runCronIsolatedAgentTurn`.

2. **Add a `beforeAttempt` hook** to `runWithModelFallback` that is called before each candidate attempt. If it returns `{ type: 'stop' }`, the fallback chain stops and preserves the original error from the previous attempt.

3. **Check remaining budget** in the cron layer's `beforeAttempt` callback. If less than `min(30s, timeout/4)` remains before the cron deadline, the fallback is skipped with a clear message:
   > `Skipping fallback: only 50ms remain before cron timeout (need at least 30000ms).`

This ensures:
- The primary model's real error is preserved (not masked by a fake cron timeout on the fallback)
- No wasted LLM API calls that would be aborted instantly
- The `beforeAttempt` hook is generic and reusable for other pre-attempt checks

## Changes

- `src/agents/model-fallback.ts` — Add `beforeAttempt` hook + `stop_before_candidate` decision type
- `src/cron/service/timer.ts` — Compute and pass `deadlineAtMs` to job execution
- `src/cron/isolated-agent/run.ts` — Use `beforeAttempt` to check remaining cron budget
- `src/cron/service/state.ts` + `src/gateway/server-cron.ts` — Thread `deadlineAtMs` through interfaces

## Tests

- `model-fallback.test.ts` — beforeAttempt stop behavior
- `run.fallback-time-budget.test.ts` — Cron deadline propagation + fallback budget exhaustion
- `service.issue-regressions.test.ts` — Deadline passed to isolated runs


## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** Cron isolated agent-turn jobs should not start a model fallback when the primary attempt has consumed almost the whole cron deadline and the fallback would be killed immediately by the same timeout.

**Real environment tested:** Local OpenClaw checkout on branch `fix/cron-fallback-timeout` at `008791fa10`, macOS host, Node 22. The proof command uses the same fallback budget formula added in this branch and the cron job shape from the affected isolated agent-turn surface.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Ran `node .artifacts/pr-52365-real-behavior-proof.mjs` locally after the patch, then ran `pnpm test src/cron/isolated-agent/run.fallback-time-budget.test.ts -- --reporter=verbose` as supplemental coverage for the same gate.

**Evidence after fix:** Terminal output from the local reproduction command:

```
$ node .artifacts/pr-52365-real-behavior-proof.mjs
cron fallback budget repro
job: sessionTarget=isolated wakeMode=next-heartbeat payload=agentTurn timeoutSeconds=60
primary attempt: consumed 59900ms of a 60000ms cron deadline
fallback check: remainingMs=100; fallbackMinRemainingMs=15000
before(upstream/main): runWithModelFallback had no beforeAttempt budget gate -> fallbackAttempted=true
after(this branch): fallbackAttempted=false
after stop: Skipping fallback: only 100ms remain before cron timeout (need at least 15000ms).
```

Supplemental targeted test output:

```
$ pnpm test src/cron/isolated-agent/run.fallback-time-budget.test.ts -- --reporter=verbose
✓ allows fallback attempts when the per-attempt budget fits inside the remaining cron deadline
✓ uses agents.defaults.timeoutSeconds for fallback budget when job timeoutSeconds is unset
✓ stops new fallback attempts when the per-attempt budget no longer fits
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  3 passed (3)
```

**Observed result after fix:** With only 100ms left before the cron deadline and a 15,000ms minimum fallback budget, the after-fix gate returns `fallbackAttempted=false` and reports `Skipping fallback: only 100ms remain before cron timeout (need at least 15000ms).` The before behavior had no `beforeAttempt` budget gate, so the fallback candidate was started even though it could only receive about 0ms.

**What was not tested:** Live Anthropic/OpenAI API calls were not run for this proof; the local reproduction covers the cron fallback budget decision and the targeted test covers the runtime hook path with mocked provider execution.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the remaining hardcoded `DEFAULT_AGENT_ID = "main"` assumptions called out in #90573 for deployments whose configured default agent is not `main`.

PR #30654 fixed the main session-key write paths, but #90573 identified follow-on paths that still synthesized `agents/main/*`, `agent:main:*`, or phantom `main` audit scopes even when config declares a different default agent such as `nova`.

This PR uses the existing `agents.list[].default` / first-agent behavior. It intentionally does **not** add a new `agents.defaultAgentId` config key or `OPENCLAW_DEFAULT_AGENT_ID` environment variable.

## Why This Change Was Made

The current behavior makes non-`main` default-agent deployments inconsistent: some surfaces honor the configured default agent, while others silently route storage, session keys, setup directories, or audit reporting through `main`. That creates broken paths and confusing phantom state for multi-agent installs.

## User Impact

Deployments whose configured default agent is not `main` can keep using their chosen default agent without residual `main` paths leaking into session initialization, auth/model storage scans, setup transcript directories, or exec-scope audit output.

## Changes

- Key new explicit `sessionId` sessions to the resolved store/default agent instead of literal `main`.
- Thread the resolved agent id into auto-reply session initialization.
- Resolve default auth/model storage scan paths from the configured default agent directory.
- Stop security audit exec-scope reporting from injecting a phantom `main` default when another agent is configured as default.
- Avoid inferring a delivery channel from one-segment agent main-session keys when the agent id happens to match a channel name.
- Let setup create the configured default agent's transcript directory instead of `agents/main/sessions` when config is available.

## Risk Mitigations

- **Compatibility:** no schema/env surface added; legacy `main` aliases are still recognized where they already were.
- **Auth-provider:** storage discovery still includes existing directories under state plus configured agent dirs; this only replaces the synthetic default path.
- **Session-state:** new explicit sessions use the same effective default agent that owns the selected store; existing persisted keys are not migrated here.

target.title: fix: persist pending followup queues across gateway restart
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #51620 — gateway restart drops queued and in-flight inbound messages.

## Changes

### New: `src/auto-reply/reply/queue/persist.ts`
Serializes all non-empty `FOLLOWUP_QUEUES` entries to `state/pending-messages.json` before shutdown. Strips non-portable fields (`config`, `skillsSnapshot`) and stores a version marker + timestamp.

### New: `src/gateway/server-pending-messages.ts`
On startup, reads the persisted file, injects missed messages as system events into their respective sessions (so the agent processes them on next turn), then deletes the file. Includes a 5-minute staleness guard to avoid replaying ancient messages from stale files.

### Modified: `src/gateway/server-close.ts`
Calls `persistFollowupQueues(FOLLOWUP_QUEUES)` before `chatRunState.clear()` so queue state is captured while still available. Best-effort — failure doesn't block shutdown.

### Modified: `src/gateway/server-startup.ts`
Calls `replayPersistedPendingMessages()` 1.5s after startup (after channels initialize), alongside the existing `scheduleRestartSentinelWake`.

## Tests

16 new tests covering:
- `persistFollowupQueues`: empty queues, non-empty queues, config stripping, multiple queues
- `consumePersistedQueues`: no file, read+delete, staleness guard (>5min), corrupt file, wrong version
- Round-trip: persist → consume
- `replayPersistedPendingMessages`: no entries, empty entries, system event injection, multiple queues, prompt truncation, empty items skip

## Limitations / Follow-up

This PR covers **Phase 1**: persisting in-memory followup queue items across restart.

Still not covered (follow-up work):
- **Phase 2**: Messages arriving during the drain window (hitting `GatewayDrainingError`) — these are rejected at the channel level before reaching the queue
- **Phase 3**: Channel-level message acknowledgment deferral — for channels that support it (Slack Socket Mode), defer ACK until message is processed or persisted so the platform can redeliver

## Testing

```
npx vitest run src/auto-reply/reply/queue/persist.test.ts src/gateway/server-pending-messages.test.ts
```

All 16 tests pass.

target.title: feat(chat-ui): syntax-highlighted code blocks and native tables in chat markdown
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Assistant messages in the shared Apple chat UI rendered fenced code without syntax highlighting and GFM tables as raw pipe characters because the whole message went through one `AttributedString(markdown:)` / `Text` pass that does not provide either surface.

Part of #100195. Addresses the table portion of #98290.

## Why This Change Was Made

The renderer now uses Swift Markdown's GFM AST to extract only top-level fenced code and tables before display. Prose retains the existing `AttributedString` path, so list and HTML containers plus document-scoped reference links keep their CommonMark semantics. Completed fenced blocks use a bounded single-pass highlighter for Swift, Kotlin, TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, Bash, and JSON; unknown, incomplete, oversized, or overlong blocks stay readable and unstyled. Tables render with native SwiftUI cells, GFM alignment, escaped pipes, short-row padding, and explicit row, column, cell, and byte limits.

The parser dependency is pinned to Swift Markdown 0.8.0, the current stable Swift.org implementation backed by cmark-gfm. Direct Swift Markdown and cmark-gfm source inspection verified source-range, table-span, container, and reference-definition behavior. Splash is Swift-focused and inactive for this broader grammar set; Highlightr adds JavaScriptCore plus bundled highlight.js grammars/themes for a six-language chat subset. The bounded in-repo tokenizer therefore remains the smaller highlighting layer while the maintained parser owns Markdown structure.

The rewrite also removes the hand-maintained block parser, makes soft-break preservation AST-aware for nested and indented code, covers Swift/Kotlin nested comments and Bash parameter expansions/redirection boundaries, caps highlighting at 200 logical lines / 20,000 UTF-8 bytes, and includes the new shared sources in the generated iOS SwiftFormat input list.

## User Impact

iOS and macOS chat show readable syntax-highlighted code cards and native aligned tables. Streaming remains responsive, source text is preserved exactly, and light/dark palettes remain dynamic.

## Evidence

- `swift test --package-path apps/shared/OpenClawKit --filter 'ChatMarkdownBlockSegmenterTests|ChatCodeHighlighterTests|ChatMarkdownDisplayPreprocessorTests'` — 72/72 passed.

target.title: fix(agents): hint when unknown tools are skills
target.body: ## Summary - **Problem:** When a model mistakenly calls a skill name as a tool (e.g. `my-skill`), the error message is a generic "Tool not found" with no guidance, so the model keeps retrying or gives up. This is especially common with weaker/smaller models that struggle to distinguish skills from tools in the system prompt. - **Why it matters:** Skills are invoked differently from tools; without a hint the model has no way to self-correct, leading to repeated failed tool calls that waste tokens and frustrate users — particularly on cost-sensitive or lower-capability model configurations. - **What changed:** Register an `afterToolCall` hook in `attempt.ts` that intercepts error tool results, detects unknown-tool errors matching a registered skill name, and rewrites the message to `Tool "X" not found. target.title: fix(process): suppress unhandled stdout/stderr stream errors in runCommandWithTimeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`runCommandWithTimeout` attaches `data` listeners to `child.stdout` and `child.stderr`, but does not attach `error` listeners. If either stream emits an `error` event (e.g., pipe read failure, premature close), the unhandled error can crash the process even though the command itself would otherwise complete normally.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add no-op `error` handlers to both stdout and stderr streams before the data handlers, mirroring the existing stdin EPIPE swallowing pattern. This prevents unhandled stream errors from propagating as uncaught exceptions.

## User Impact

More robust subprocess execution: transient stream read errors no longer crash the OpenClaw process.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test in `src/process/exec.test.ts` that emits `error` events on both stdout and stderr and verifies `runCommandWithTimeout` still resolves successfully.
- Verified the test fails on `main` with `Error: stdout read failed` and passes with this fix.
- `oxlint` passes on the changed files.
